claim: The study generated single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles of 90,980 nuclei from human lungs.
source: Here, we present single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles of 90,980 nuclei and matched single-nucleus transcriptomes of 46,500 nuclei in non-diseased lungs from donors of ~30 weeks gestation,~3 years and ~30 years.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of nuclei profiled using snATAC-seq.

claim: The study generated matched single-nucleus transcriptomes of 46,500 nuclei from human lungs.
source: Here, we present single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles of 90,980 nuclei and matched single-nucleus transcriptomes of 46,500 nuclei in non-diseased lungs from donors of ~30 weeks gestation,~3 years and ~30 years.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of nuclei profiled using snRNA-seq.

claim: The lung samples came from donors of approximately 30 weeks gestation, 3 years, and 30 years of age.
source: Here, we present single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles of 90,980 nuclei and matched single-nucleus transcriptomes of 46,500 nuclei in non-diseased lungs from donors of ~30 weeks gestation,~3 years and ~30 years.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the age groups of donors.

claim: The study mapped candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) in human lungs.
source: We mapped candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) and linked them to putative target genes.
evidence: The abstract states that cCREs were mapped.

claim: Candidate cis-regulatory elements were linked to putative target genes.
source: We mapped candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) and linked them to putative target genes.
evidence: The abstract states that cCREs were linked to target genes.

claim: Distal cCREs with age-increased activity were identified that are linked to TMPRSS2 in alveolar type 2 cells.
source: We identified distal cCREs with age-increased activity linked to SARS-CoV-2 host entry gene TMPRSS2 in alveolar type 2 cells, which had immune regulatory signatures and harbored variants associated with respiratory traits.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: The distal cCREs linked to TMPRSS2 in AT2 cells had immune regulatory signatures.
source: We identified distal cCREs with age-increased activity linked to SARS-CoV-2 host entry gene TMPRSS2 in alveolar type 2 cells, which had immune regulatory signatures and harbored variants associated with respiratory traits.
evidence: The abstract states that these cCREs had immune regulatory signatures.

claim: The distal cCREs linked to TMPRSS2 in AT2 cells harbored variants associated with respiratory traits.
source: We identified distal cCREs with age-increased activity linked to SARS-CoV-2 host entry gene TMPRSS2 in alveolar type 2 cells, which had immune regulatory signatures and harbored variants associated with respiratory traits.
evidence: The abstract states that these cCREs harbored variants associated with respiratory traits.

claim: A candidate variant at the 3p21.31 COVID-19 risk locus overlapped a distal cCRE linked to SLC6A20.
source: At the 3p21.31 COVID-19 risk locus, a candidate variant overlapped a distal cCRE linked to SLC6A20, a gene expressed in alveolar cells and with known functional association with the SARS-CoV-2 receptor ACE2.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: SLC6A20 is expressed in alveolar cells.
source: At the 3p21.31 COVID-19 risk locus, a candidate variant overlapped a distal cCRE linked to SLC6A20, a gene expressed in alveolar cells and with known functional association with the SARS-CoV-2 receptor ACE2.
evidence: The abstract states that SLC6A20 is expressed in alveolar cells.

claim: SLC6A20 has a known functional association with the SARS-CoV-2 receptor ACE2.
source: At the 3p21.31 COVID-19 risk locus, a candidate variant overlapped a distal cCRE linked to SLC6A20, a gene expressed in alveolar cells and with known functional association with the SARS-CoV-2 receptor ACE2.
evidence: The abstract states that SLC6A20 has a known functional association with ACE2.

claim: Respiratory failure associated with COVID-19 has placed focus on the lungs.
source: Respiratory failure associated with COVID-19 has placed focus on the lungs.
evidence: The introduction states this as context for the study.

claim: The lungs act as a critical barrier that protects against inhaled pathogens such as viruses.
source: Not only do the lungs act as a critical barrier that protects against inhaled pathogens such as viruses, it is also a site of many COVID-19 symptoms including the primary cause of COVID-19 mortality, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: The lungs are a site of many COVID-19 symptoms including acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
source: Not only do the lungs act as a critical barrier that protects against inhaled pathogens such as viruses, it is also a site of many COVID-19 symptoms including the primary cause of COVID-19 mortality, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the primary cause of COVID-19 mortality.
source: Not only do the lungs act as a critical barrier that protects against inhaled pathogens such as viruses, it is also a site of many COVID-19 symptoms including the primary cause of COVID-19 mortality, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: An average human adult lung has an estimated 480 million alveoli.
source: In an average human adult lungs, an estimated 480 million alveoli give rise to approximately 140 m2 of gas-exchange surface area (Ochs et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this anatomical fact.

claim: The alveoli in human adult lungs give rise to approximately 140 m2 of gas-exchange surface area.
source: In an average human adult lungs, an estimated 480 million alveoli give rise to approximately 140 m2 of gas-exchange surface area (Ochs et al., 2004).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this anatomical fact.

claim: Respiratory epithelial cells are at the frontline of infection.
source: Respiratory epithelial cells are at the frontline of infection, although some pathogens that have bypassed the barrier can infect other cell types.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: The human airway epithelium is composed of luminal cells and basal cells.
source: The human airway epithelium is composed of luminal cells and basal cells (Tata and Rajagopal, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this anatomical fact.

claim: Luminal cells include club cells and goblet cells that moisturize the air and trap pathogens.
source: Luminal cells include club cells and goblet cells that moisturize the air and trap pathogens, as well as ciliated cells that sweep out inhaled particles.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Luminal cells include ciliated cells that sweep out inhaled particles.
source: Luminal cells include club cells and goblet cells that moisturize the air and trap pathogens, as well as ciliated cells that sweep out inhaled particles.
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Basal cells serve as progenitors when luminal cells are lost after infection.
source: These luminal cells are underlined by basal cells, which serve as progenitors when luminal cells are lost after infection (Hogan et al., 2014; Kim, 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this biological function.

claim: The alveolar epithelium is composed of alveolar type 1 cells (AT1s) and alveolar type 2 cells (AT2s).
source: The alveolar epithelium is composed of alveolar type 1 cells (AT1s), which are flat and line the gas–blood interface to facilitate gas exchange; and alveolar type 2 cells (AT2s), which produce surfactant to reduce surface tension and protect against pathogens (Whitsett and Weaver, 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this anatomical fact.

claim: AT1 cells are flat and line the gas-blood interface to facilitate gas exchange.
source: The alveolar epithelium is composed of alveolar type 1 cells (AT1s), which are flat and line the gas–blood interface to facilitate gas exchange; and alveolar type 2 cells (AT2s), which produce surfactant to reduce surface tension and protect against pathogens (Whitsett and Weaver, 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this biological function.

claim: AT2 cells produce surfactant to reduce surface tension and protect against pathogens.
source: The alveolar epithelium is composed of alveolar type 1 cells (AT1s), which are flat and line the gas–blood interface to facilitate gas exchange; and alveolar type 2 cells (AT2s), which produce surfactant to reduce surface tension and protect against pathogens (Whitsett and Weaver, 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this biological function.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 likely infects both the airway and alveolar regions of the lungs.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 likely infects both the airway and alveolar regions of the lungs, it is the damage to the alveolar region that causes ARDS (Du et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this claim about SARS-CoV-2 infection.

claim: Damage to the alveolar region causes ARDS in COVID-19.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 likely infects both the airway and alveolar regions of the lungs, it is the damage to the alveolar region that causes ARDS (Du et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this claim.

claim: There are several large-scale studies using single-cell transcriptomics to define cell types within human lungs.
source: There are several large-scale studies, including efforts from LungMap and the Human Cell Atlas, which aim to define cell types within the human lungs using single-cell transcriptomics as the central modality (Reyfman et al., 2019; Schiller et al., 2019; Travaglini et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for these studies.

claim: There is a paucity of single-cell data focused on mapping cis-regulatory elements (CREs) in the human genome that are active in specific lung cell types.
source: In contrast, there is a paucity of single-cell data focused on mapping cis-regulatory elements (CREs) in the human genome that are active in specific lung cell types.
evidence: The introduction states this as a gap in the literature.

claim: CREs associate with combinations of transcription factors to drive spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression.
source: CREs associate with combinations of transcription factors to drive spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression (Moore et al., 2020) and enable cell-specific responses to intra- and extra-cellular signals, for example, aging (Booth and Brunet, 2016) and inflammation (Smale and Natoli, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this biological mechanism.

claim: CREs enable cell-specific responses to aging and inflammation.
source: CREs associate with combinations of transcription factors to drive spatiotemporal patterns of gene expression (Moore et al., 2020) and enable cell-specific responses to intra- and extra-cellular signals, for example, aging (Booth and Brunet, 2016) and inflammation (Smale and Natoli, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this biological mechanism.

claim: Complex disease-associated variants identified in GWAS are enriched in CREs.
source: Furthermore, complex disease-associated variants identified in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are enriched in CREs (Maurano et al., 2015; Pickrell, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this finding.

claim: Accessible or 'open' chromatin is a hallmark of CREs.
source: Accessible or 'open' chromatin is a hallmark of CREs and can be used to localize candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs).
evidence: The introduction states this as established knowledge.

claim: Chromatin accessibility can be assayed using DNase-seq and ATAC-seq.
source: Chromatin accessibility can be assayed using 'bulk' or 'ensemble' techniques such as DNase-seq and ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Thurman et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites references for these techniques.

claim: Single-cell ATAC-seq has been developed to map the epigenome and gene regulatory programs within component cell types.
source: To overcome limitations regarding tissue heterogeneity inherent in such assays, technologies such like single-cell ATAC-seq have been developed to map the epigenome and gene regulatory programs within component cell types (Buenrostro et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2018; Cusanovich et al., 2015; Cusanovich et al., 2018; Lareau et al., 2019; Satpathy et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for this technology.

claim: Accessible chromatin profiles derived from single cells can elucidate cell-type-specific cCREs.
source: Accessible chromatin profiles derived from single cells can elucidate cell-type-specific cCREs, transcriptional regulators driving element activity, and putative target genes linked to distal cCREs through single-cell co-accessibility (Cusanovich et al., 2018; Lareau et al., 2019; Pliner et al., 2018; Preissl et al., 2018; Satpathy et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for this capability.

claim: Human sequence variants affecting complex traits and diseases are enriched in non-coding sequences.
source: Importantly, human sequence variants affecting complex traits and diseases are enriched in non-coding sequences (Maurano et al., 2015; Pickrell, 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this finding.

claim: Cell-type-specific profiles derived from single-cell chromatin accessibility data can help prioritize the cell types of action and function of disease variants.
source: Thus, cell-type-specific profiles derived from single-cell chromatin accessibility data can help prioritize the cell types of action and function of these variants (Chiou et al., 2019; Corces et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this application.

claim: CDC data has consistently demonstrated that the rate of hospitalization or death from COVID-19 is significantly lower among children compared to adults or elderly individuals.
source: Epidemiology data of US cases reported by the CDC has consistently demonstrated that the rate of hospitalization or death from COVID-19 is significantly lower among children compared to adults or elderly individuals, amidst caution that children can still be infected and transmit the virus (CDC, 2020a; CDC, 2020b).
evidence: The introduction cites CDC reports for this epidemiological finding.

claim: Children can still be infected with SARS-CoV-2 and transmit the virus.
source: Epidemiology data of US cases reported by the CDC has consistently demonstrated that the rate of hospitalization or death from COVID-19 is significantly lower among children compared to adults or elderly individuals, amidst caution that children can still be infected and transmit the virus (CDC, 2020a; CDC, 2020b).
evidence: The introduction cites CDC reports for this caution.

claim: Age-associated differences in COVID-19 outcomes may be due to different expression levels of viral entry proteins and different immune resilience to viral infection.
source: There are likely many reasons that underlie the age-associated differences, including different expression levels of viral entry proteins and different immune resilience to viral infection.
evidence: The introduction speculates on possible reasons for age differences.

claim: ACE2 has been demonstrated as the receptor for SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2.
source: ACE2 has been demonstrated as the receptor for not only the original SARS-CoV, but also SARS-CoV-2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Lan et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for this finding.

claim: TMPRSS2 and CTSL cleave the viral spike protein, thereby facilitating fusion of the virus with host cells.
source: Based on literature from the original SARS-CoV as well as emerging data from SARS-CoV-2, TMPRSS2 and CTSL cleave the viral spike protein, thereby facilitate fusion of the virus with host cells (Huang et al., 2006; Matsuyama et al., 2020; Reinke et al., 2017; Walls et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for this mechanism.

claim: TMPRSS2 has been shown to be essential for coronavirus viral entry while CTSL is dispensable.
source: In particular, TMPRSS2 has been shown to be essential for coronavirus viral entry while CTSL is dispensable (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Shirato et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple references for this finding.

claim: BSG encodes a receptor that can bind to the SARS-CoV spike protein.
source: BSG encodes another receptor that can bind to the SARS-CoV spike protein (Chen et al., 2005) and FURIN encodes a protease with a putative target site in SARS-CoV-2, adding both genes to the list of host machinery highjacked by the virus (Coutard et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this finding.

claim: FURIN encodes a protease with a putative target site in SARS-CoV-2.
source: BSG encodes another receptor that can bind to the SARS-CoV spike protein (Chen et al., 2005) and FURIN encodes a protease with a putative target site in SARS-CoV-2, adding both genes to the list of host machinery highjacked by the virus (Coutard et al., 2020; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites references for this finding.

claim: The study generated donor-matched single-nucleus RNA-seq and single-nucleus ATAC-seq data across neonatal, pediatric, and adult lungs with three donors in each group.
source: To contribute to our understanding of gene regulation in the human lungs during aging and how such regulation goes awry and contributes to disease, including SARS-CoV-2 infection, we generated donor-matched single-nucleus RNA-seq and single-nucleus ATAC-seq data across neonatal, pediatric, and adult lungs with three donors in each group.
evidence: The introduction states the study design.

claim: The study profiled gene expression dynamics at cell-type resolution of SARS-CoV-2 host entry genes ACE2, TMPRSS2, CTSL, BSG, and FURIN.
source: Using these datasets, we profiled gene expression dynamics at cell-type resolution of SARS-CoV-2 host entry genes ACE2, TMPRSS2, CTSL, BSG, and FURIN and revealed cCREs underlying these changes for ACE2 and TMPRSS2, genes that encode the primary receptor and fusion protein.
evidence: The introduction states this as a study objective and finding.

claim: The study revealed cCREs underlying changes in ACE2 and TMPRSS2 expression.
source: Using these datasets, we profiled gene expression dynamics at cell-type resolution of SARS-CoV-2 host entry genes ACE2, TMPRSS2, CTSL, BSG, and FURIN and revealed cCREs underlying these changes for ACE2 and TMPRSS2, genes that encode the primary receptor and fusion protein.
evidence: The introduction states this as a study finding.

claim: The study profiled non-coding sequence variation in cCREs associated with TMPRSS2 that may impact regulatory activity.
source: We further profiled non-coding sequence variation in cCREs associated with TMPRSS2 that may impact regulatory activity and might contribute to differential susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection by affecting TMPRSS2 expression.
evidence: The introduction states this as a study objective.

claim: The study annotated the 3p21.31 COVID-19 risk locus.
source: Finally, we demonstrated the value of this resource in interpreting emerging genetic risk of respiratory failure in COVID-19 by annotating the recently identified 3p21.31 locus (Ellinghaus et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction states this as a study finding and cites the source of the risk locus.

claim: After batch correction and filtering, 90,980 single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles were analyzed.
source: After batch correction and filtering of low-quality nuclei and likely doublets, we clustered and analyzed a total of 90,980 single-nucleus accessible chromatin profiles (Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section states the number of nuclei analyzed after QC.

claim: 19 clusters were identified representing epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial, and hematopoietic cell types.
source: We identified 19 clusters representing epithelial (AT1-alveolar type 1, AT2-alveolar type 2, club, ciliated, basal, and pulmonary neuroendocrine), mesenchymal (myofibroblast, pericyte, matrix fibroblast 1, and matrix fibroblast 2), endothelial (arterial, lymphatic, capillary 1 and capillary 2), and hematopoietic cell types (macrophage, B-cell, T-cell, NK cell, and enucleated erythrocyte) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The results section states the number and types of clusters identified, referencing Figure 1A.

claim: Cell-type-specific patterns of chromatin accessibility were observed at known marker genes for each cell type.
source: Supporting these cluster annotations, we observed cell-type-specific patterns of chromatin accessibility at known marker genes for each cell type (Figure 1B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The results section states this observation, referencing figures.

claim: 46,500 single-nucleus transcriptomes passed QC criteria from the donor and sample-matched snRNA-seq data.
source: We similarly clustered the 46,500 single-nucleus transcriptomes, which passed QC criteria from the donor and sample-matched snRNA-seq data (Figure 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The results section states the number of transcriptomes analyzed after QC.

claim: snRNA-seq clusters represented all major cell types in the small airway region of the lungs.
source: These clusters represented all major cell types in the small airway region of the lungs (Figure 1C,D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: snRNA-seq clusters overlapped those identified from snATAC-seq.
source: Importantly, these clusters overlapped those identified from snATAC-seq, highlighted by a cluster of rare pulmonary neuroendocrine cells (PNECs) represented in both modalities (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: ACE2 transcript was detected in very few nuclei (total 80 nuclei) in the normal lungs.
source: We detected ACE2 transcript in very few nuclei (total 80 nuclei) in the normal lungs and these nuclei were enriched within the epithelial lineage (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: ACE2-expressing nuclei were enriched within the epithelial lineage.
source: We detected ACE2 transcript in very few nuclei (total 80 nuclei) in the normal lungs and these nuclei were enriched within the epithelial lineage (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: Low ACE2 expression in multiple tissues is consistent with recent publications.
source: This is consistent with exceptionally low ACE2 expression in multiple tissues analyzed in recent publications (Muus et al., 2020; Qi et al., 2020; Sungnak et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020; Ziegler et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section cites multiple references for this consistency.

claim: AT2 cells had the highest number of ACE2+ nuclei, accounting for 48.8% of all ACE2-expressing nuclei (39 out of total 80 ACE2+ nuclei).
source: In our data, AT2 cells had the highest number of ACE2+ nuclei, accounting for 48.8% of all ACE2-expressing nuclei (39 out of total 80 ACE2+ nuclei) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific numbers, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: TMPRSS2 transcripts were detected in many more cells (total 6547 nuclei) compared to ACE2.
source: In comparison, TMPRSS2 transcripts were detected in many more cells (total 6547 nuclei, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific numbers, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: Most TMPRSS2-expressing cells were epithelial cells including AT1 and AT2 cells and airway cells such as club, ciliated and goblet cells.
source: Most TMPRSS2-expressing cells were epithelial cells including AT1 and AT2 cells and airway cells such as club, ciliated and goblet cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: TMPRSS2 was detected in 3,315/7,226 nuclei, or 45.8% of the AT2 cells.
source: Within the AT2 population, TMPRSS2 was detected in 3,315/7,226 nuclei, or 45.8% of the AT2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific numbers, referencing a figure.

claim: 21 of the 39 ACE+ AT2 cells also expressed TMPRSS2.
source: Importantly, 21 of the 39 ACE+ AT2 cells also expressed TMPRSS2 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific numbers, referencing a supplementary file.

claim: CTSL, BSG and FURIN were expressed in a large number of AT1, AT2, matrix fibroblast1,2, and M1 macrophage cells.
source: The other three candidate genes of SARS-CoV-2 host cell entry CTSL, BSG and FURIN were expressed in a large number of AT1, AT2, matrix fibroblast1,2, and M1 macrophage cells, as well as a small number of cells in additional cell types (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: ACE2 and TMPRSS2 were primarily accessible throughout their gene body in alveolar cells such as AT1, AT2, and airway cells such as club, ciliated, and basal cells.
source: Consistent with their gene expression, both ACE2 and TMPRSS2 were primarily accessible throughout their gene body in alveolar cells such as AT1, AT2, and airway cells such as club, ciliated, and basal cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: The CTSL gene body exhibited chromatin accessibility across epithelial cells, mesenchymal cells, endothelial cells, and macrophages.
source: Conversely, the CTSL gene body exhibited chromatin accessibility across epithelial cells, mesenchymal cells, endothelial cells, and macrophages (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: BSG and FURIN showed broad chromatin accessibility patterns with the highest activity in endothelial cells, such as capillaries.
source: BSG and FURIN also showed broad chromatin accessibility patterns with the highest activity in endothelial cells, such as capillaries (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: Both the airway and alveolar epithelial cells express genes critical for SARS-CoV-2 entry.
source: Together, both gene expression and chromatin accessibility suggest that among cell types constituting the barrier exposed to inhaled pathogens, both the airway and alveolar epithelial cells express genes critical for SARS-CoV-2 entry.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on the data.

claim: 398,385 cCREs were mapped across all lung cell types.
source: Overall, we mapped 398,385 cCREs across all lung cell types.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: 15 sites co-accessible with the ACE2 promoter were identified.
source: At the ACE2 locus, we identified 15 sites co-accessible with the ACE2 promoter (Figure 2C,D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: The modest number of co-accessible sites at ACE2 is likely due to the small percentage of ACE2+ nuclei.
source: We speculate that the modest number of co-accessible sites is likely due to the small percentage of ACE2+ nuclei (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section speculates on the reason for the finding.

claim: 73 accessible chromatin sites co-accessible with the TMPRSS2 promoter were identified.
source: In comparison, at the TMPRSS2 locus, we identified 73 accessible chromatin sites co-accessible with the TMPRSS2 promoter (Figure 2E,F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: 73, 213, and 64 accessible chromatin sites co-accessible with CTSL, FURIN, and BSG promoters were identified, respectively.
source: Finally, at the CTSL, FURIN, and BSG loci we identified 73, 213, and 64 accessible chromatin sites co-accessible with their respective gene promoters (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a supplementary file.

claim: A higher fraction of AT2 cells expressing ACE2 and TMPRSS2 was observed in adult lungs compared to pediatric samples.
source: We observed a higher fraction of AT2 cells expressing ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in adult lungs as compared to pediatric samples in our small cohort (n = 3 per age group, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The results section states this observation, referencing figures.

claim: The observed age-related increase in expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is consistent with findings from a parallel report by the Human Cell Atlas.
source: Notably, these observed age-related increase in expression of these two genes is consistent with findings from a parallel report spearheaded by the Human Cell Atlas (HCA) that included pediatric data as part of a large-scale meta-analysis (Muus et al., 2020; Schuler et al., 2020).
evidence: The results section cites references for this consistency.

claim: The expression levels per nucleus for ACE2 and TMPRSS2 were similar across different age groups.
source: In contrast to the percentage of AT2 cells expressing these genes, the expression levels per nucleus were similar across different age groups for either ACE2 (no nucleus had >1 UMI detected) or TMPRSS2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: No age-related trend was observed for BSG, CTSL, FURIN.
source: Notably, we did not observe an age-related trend for the other candidate viral entry genes BSG, CTSL, FURIN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: 22,745 age-linked sites in AT2 cells were identified, which exhibited significant differences (FDR < 0.05) in any pairwise comparison.
source: Overall, we identified 22,745 age-linked sites in AT2 cells, which exhibited significant differences (FDR < 0.05) in any pairwise comparison (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: Clustering of dynamic peaks revealed five predominant groups of age-linked chromatin accessibility patterns (cI-cV).
source: Clustering of these dynamic peaks revealed five predominant groups of age-linked chromatin accessibility patterns (cI-cV, Figure 3E).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: Two clusters of AT2 sites exhibited increasing accessibility with age including nine sites co-accessible with TMPRSS2 (cIII 30yo enriched and cIV 3yo + 30yo).
source: Of these dynamic peaks, we identified two clusters of AT2 sites exhibiting increasing accessibility with age including several sites linked to candidate genes for SARS-CoV-2 host genes, most notably nine sites co-accessible with TMPRSS2 (cIII 30yo enriched and cIV 3yo + 30yo, Figure 3E).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: The two age-increasing co-accessible site containing clusters were enriched for processes related to viral infection, immune response and injury repair.
source: Intriguingly, these two age-increasing co-accessible site containing clusters were enriched for processes related to viral infection, immune response and injury repair such as viral release from host cell, interferon-gamma mediated signaling pathway, and positive regulation of ERBB signaling pathway (Figure 3F, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: The age-dependent clusters were enriched for phenotypes substantiated in mouse studies, such as pulmonary epithelial necrosis, increased monocyte cell number, and chronic inflammation.
source: Also, these age-dependent clusters were enriched for phenotypes substantiated in mouse studies, such as pulmonary epithelial necrosis, increased monocyte cell number, and chronic inflammation (Figure 3F, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: An enrichment of sequence motifs within age-dependent clusters was observed for transcription factors controlling endoderm cell fate (FOXA, HNF1), lung cell fate (NKX), AT2 cell fate (CEBP) and AT2 cell signaling (ETS).
source: We observed an enrichment of sequence motifs within these clusters for transcription factors controlling endoderm cell fate (FOXA, HNF1), lung cell fate (NKX), AT2 cell fate (CEBP) and AT2 cell signaling (ETS) (Maeda et al., 2007; Morrisey et al., 2013; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites references for the TF functions.

claim: An enrichment of motifs for factors involved in immune signaling such as STAT, IRF, and FOS/JUN was observed in age-dependent clusters.
source: Further supporting immune regulation of AT2 cell gene expression, we observed an enrichment of motifs for factors involved in immune signaling such as STAT, IRF, and FOS/JUN (Au-Yeung and Horvath, 2018; Mogensen, 2018; Figure 3G, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites references for the TF functions, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: 19 age-increasing TMPRSS2-linked cCREs were identified, 17 of which were statistically significant (FDR < 0.05 via EdgeR and/or p<0.05 via independent t-test).
source: Overall, we identified 10 additional cCREs co-accessible with TMPRSS2, which exhibited patterns of increasing accessibility with age for a total of 19 age-increasing TMPRSS2-linked cCREs, 17 of which were statistically significant, with the caveat of modest sample size (N = 3 per age group) (FDR < 0.05 via EdgeR and/or p<0.05 via independent t-test, Figure 3H,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: Accessibility at the TMPRSS2 promoter did not exhibit differential accessibility with age.
source: Notably, accessibility at the TMPRSS2 promoter did not exhibit differential accessibility with age (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) emphasizing a likely role of distal cCREs in regulating age-increasing TMPRSS2 expression in AT2 cells.
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: 2270 non-singleton sequence variants in the gnomAD v3 database overlapped age-increasing cCREs linked to TMPRSS2 in AT2s.
source: In total, 2270 non-singleton sequence variants in the gnomAD v3 database (Karczewski et al., 2019) overlapped age-increasing cCREs linked to TMPRSS2 in AT2s.
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites the database.

claim: 1100 variants were identified in a predicted motif for one or more of CEBP, ETS, NKX, FOXA, IRF and STAT TFs.
source: In total we identified 1100 variants in a predicted motif for one or more of these TFs (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: 212 variants with significant predicted effects (FDR < 0.1) on AT2 chromatin accessibility were identified using deltaSVM.
source: We further applied a machine learning approach (deltaSVM) (Lee et al., 2015) to model AT2 chromatin accessibility and identified 212 variants with significant predicted effects (FDR < 0.1) on AT2 chromatin accessibility (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites the method, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: Among motif-bound variants, 50 were common (MAF>1%) of which 10 further had predicted effects on AT2 chromatin accessibility using deltaSVM.
source: Among motif-bound variants, 50 were common (defined here as minor allele frequency [MAF]>1%) of which 10 further had predicted effects on AT2 chromatin accessibility using deltaSVM (Lee et al., 2015; Figure 4A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites the method, referencing figures and supplementary files.

claim: Common variants with predicted function generally had consistent frequencies across populations, although multiple variants, for example rs35074065, were much less common in East Asians (MAF = 0.005) relative to other populations (Europeans MAF = 0.45, South Asian MAF = 0.37, African MAF = 0.12).
source: Common variants with predicted function generally had consistent frequencies across populations, although multiple variants, for example rs35074065, were much less common in East Asians (MAF = 0.005) relative to other populations (Europeans MAF = 0.45, South Asian MAF = 0.37, African MAF = 0.12).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific allele frequencies.

claim: The majority of common variants with predicted AT2 effects (9/10) were nominally associated (p<1×10−2) with at least one phenotype related to respiratory function or respiratory medication use.
source: Furthermore, the majority of these variants (9/10) were nominally associated (p<1×10−2) with at least one phenotype related to respiratory function or respiratory medication use including bronchiectasis (rs462903 p=2.0 × 10−4, rs9974995 p=7.1 × 10−4), bacterial pneumonia (rs2838089 p=2.4×10−4), COPD (rs1557372 p=2.9 × 10−3), asthma (rs8127290 p=1.4×10−3) and medications used to treat asthma such as serevent (rs220266 p=3.1×10−4, rs62219349 p-5.3 × 10−3) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific p-values, referencing a figure.

claim: A highly significant eQTL for TMPRSS2 expression was observed at rs35074065 (p=3.9 × 10−11) in GTEx v8 lung data.
source: Among variants tested for association in GTEx, we observed a highly significant eQTL for TMPRSS2 expression at rs35074065 (p=3.9 × 10−11) as well as more nominal eQTL evidence at rs1557372 (p=2.9 × 10−5) and rs9974995 (p=3.5 × 10−6).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific p-values.

claim: In fine-mapping data from GTEx, rs35074065 had a high posterior probability (PPA = 41.6%) and therefore likely has a direct causal effect on TMPRSS2 expression.
source: Furthermore, in fine-mapping data from GTEx, rs35074065 had a high posterior probability (PPA = 41.6%) and therefore likely has a direct casual effect on TMPRSS2 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section states this finding and inference, referencing a figure.

claim: The variant rs35074065 disrupted predicted sequence motifs for IRF and STAT transcription factors, where the TMPRSS2-increasing allele disrupted motif binding.
source: This variant further disrupted predicted sequence motifs for IRF and STAT transcription factors, where the TMPRSS2-increasing allele disrupted motif binding, suggesting that its effects may be mediated through interferon signaling and anti-viral programs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section states this finding and speculation, referencing a figure.

claim: Highly significant association was observed between rs35074065 and TMPRSS2 expression when including AT2 cell proportion (p=3.8 × 10−18) as well as macrophage proportion (p=4.0 × 10−12) in the eQTL model.
source: We observed highly significant association when including AT2 cell proportion (p=3.8 × 10−18) as well as macrophage proportion (p=4.0 × 10−12), supporting the possibility that the TMPRSS2 eQTL at rs35074065 acts through AT2 cells and macrophages, which is in line with TMPRSS2-expressing cell types in the lungs (Figure 4E, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific p-values, referencing figures.

claim: Fine-mapping of the 3p21.31 signal resulted in 22 total candidate causal variants.
source: Fine-mapping of the 3p21.31 signal resulted in 22 total candidate causal variants.
evidence: The results section states this finding.

claim: Two fine-mapped variants overlapped a lung cell-type cCRE: rs17713054 (PPA=0.04), which mapped in a cCRE accessible in epithelial and mesenchymal cells with the highest signal in AT2 cells, and rs76374459, (PPA = 0.02), which mapped in a cCRE accessible in erythrocytes.
source: Among these, two fine-mapped variants overlapped a lung cell-type cCRE: rs17713054 (posterior probability [PPA]=0.04), which mapped in a cCRE accessible in epithelial (AT1/2, basal, club, ciliated) and mesenchymal (matrix fibroblast 1/2, myofibroblast) cells with the highest signal in AT2 cells, and rs76374459, (PPA = 0.02), which mapped in a cCRE accessible in erythrocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: For rs17713054, the minor (and risk increasing) allele A was predicted to bind CEBPA and CEBPB motifs.
source: For rs17713054, the minor (and risk increasing) allele A was predicted to bind CEBPA and CEBPB motifs (Figure 5B), which were broadly enriched in age-related cCREs in AT2 cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing figures.

claim: The variant rs17713054 overlapped a CEBPB ChIP-seq site identified in the ENCODE project.
source: In further support of CEBP binding to this locus, this variant overlapped a CEBPB ChIP-seq site identified in the ENCODE project (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites references, referencing a figure.

claim: At rs76374459, the risk allele C was predicted to disrupt binding of SPI1 among other TFs and overlapped a SPI1 ChIP-seq site in ENCODE.
source: At rs76374459, the risk allele C was predicted to disrupt binding of SPI1 among other TFs and overlapped a SPI1 ChIP-seq site in ENCODE (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites references, referencing a figure.

claim: Candidate causal variants at the 3p21.31 signal showed evidence for nominal association with respiratory phenotypes for example bronchiectasis medication (rs76374459 p=2.0×10−3), emphysema (rs17713054 p=1.4×10−2), and chronic bronchitis (rs17712877 p=1.1×10−2).
source: Candidate causal variants at the 3p21.31 signal also showed evidence for nominal association with respiratory phenotypes for example bronchiectasis medication (rs76374459 p=2.0×10−3), emphysema (rs17713054 p=1.4×10−2), and chronic bronchitis (rs17712877 p=1.1×10−2), among other associations.
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific p-values.

claim: The site harboring rs17713054 was co-accessible with the promoter region of multiple genes including SLC6A20, LIMD1, SACM1L, and CCRL2.
source: The site harboring rs17713054 was co-accessible with the promoter region of multiple genes including SLC6A20, LIMD1, SACM1L, and CCRL2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: SLC6A20 was expressed predominantly in AT2 cells and had low expression in other cell types.
source: Among these genes, SLC6A20, which encodes a proline transporter, was expressed predominantly in AT2 cells and had low expression in other cell types (Figure 5D).
evidence: The results section states this finding, referencing a figure.

claim: Nominal association was observed between rs17713054 and SLC6A20 expression where the minor (and risk increasing) allele A had increased expression (p=8.09 × 10−3).
source: While there were no significant associations, we observed nominal association with SLC6A20 where the minor (and risk increasing) allele A had increased expression (p=8.09 × 10−3).
evidence: The results section states this finding with a specific p-value.

claim: Strongest association between rs17713054 and SLC6A20 expression was observed when including AT2 or AT1/AT2-like cell proportion (p=4.09 × 10−3, p=8.00 × 10−4).
source: We observed strongest association when including AT2 or AT1/AT2-like cell proportion (p=4.09 × 10−3, p=8.00 × 10−4) (Figure 5E), supporting the possibility that rs17713054 regulates SLC6A20 expression in AT2 cells.
evidence: The results section states this finding with specific p-values, referencing a figure.

source: In Xenopus oocytes, ACE2 expression promotes SLC6A20 protein levels, localization to plasma membrane and its function in proline amino acid transport (Vuille-dit-Bille et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference for this finding.

claim: In Ace2 mutant mice, proline transport, presumably via SLC6A20, was severely disrupted.
source: Conversely, in Ace2 mutant mice, proline transport, presumably via SLC6A20, was severely disrupted (Singer et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference for this finding.

claim: ACE2 is required for protecting the lungs from injury-induced acute respiratory distress phenotypes.
source: Aside from being a viral receptor gene, ACE2 is also required for protecting the lungs from injury-induced acute respiratory distress phenotypes, the precise cause of COVID-19 mortality (Imai et al., 2005).
evidence: The discussion cites a reference for this finding.

claim: Tmprss2 mutant mice show no defects at baseline and are more resistant to the original SARS-CoV infection.
source: In comparison, Tmprss2 mutant mice show no defects at baseline and are more resistant to the original SARS-CoV infection (Iwata-Yoshikawa et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: The discussion cites references for this finding.

claim: TMPRSS2 is involved in the entry of other respiratory viruses such as influenza.
source: TMPRSS2 is also involved in the entry of other respiratory viruses such as influenza, suggesting that modulating its expression may also be effective in deterring entry and spread of other viruses (Limburg et al., 2019).
